Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 45, verses 7–11:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Woe to every sinful liar.﴾ ﴿He hears the verses of Allah recited to him, yet he persists in arrogance, as though he had not heard them. So give him the tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And when he learns something of Our verses, he takes them in mockery. For those there is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿Before them lies Hell, and what they earned will not avail them at all, nor those they took as protectors besides Allah. For them is a tremendous punishment.﴾ ﴿This is guidance, and those who disbelieve in the verses of their Lord, for them is a punishment of painful wretchedness.﴾

"Al-Waylu" (woe) in the speech of the Arabs means calamities, sorrow, grief, distress, and hardship, among these meanings. It is a word used in invoking a curse upon a person. It has been narrated in some reports that in Hell there is a valley named Wayl. al-Tabari held that what is meant in the verse, and what the language requires, is an invocation against the people of falsehood and sin with the meanings mentioned earlier. Al-Affak is the great liar, the one from whom falsehood proceeds repeatedly. Al-Athim is an intensive form (ism fa'il of the intensive pattern) from athima, yref ya'thamu.

It has been narrated that the occasion of this verse was Abu Jahl; it was also said to be al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The correct view is that its occasion is what those mentioned and others did, and that it encompasses everyone who falls under the described attributes until the Day of Resurrection.

"Yusirru" means he remains firm upon his creed of disbelief. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿so give him the tidings of a painful punishment﴾ is apt, because it has made the punishment explicit; if the tidings were not restricted to anything, they would apply only to the beloved (ones).

The majority of reciters read: ﴿"wa-idha 'alima"﴾ with a fatha on the ʿayn and a light lam, meaning: when he is informed of something of Our verses, he knows the report itself, not the meaning it contains. Had he known the meanings contained in the reports of the Shariah and the reality of their truths, he would have been a believer. Qatada and Matar al-Warraq read "wa-idha ʿulima" (p-592) with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the lam. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"ulaika"﴾ refers back to the expression "every sinful liar," because it is a collective noun to which the attributes mentioned afterward belong.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Before them lies Hell﴾: some exegetes said its meaning is "from in front of them." This is like the disagreement over His saying: ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾ [al-Kahf: 79]. The one who holds this view takes the matter as follows: a person, in the course of his life, moves toward a garden or a fire, so both are before him. But the word "al-Wara'" in the language does not mean that; it means what comes behind a person. If the matter is considered in terms of precedence or subsequence in existence, since time is like a path for things, the matter is consistent: whatever comes after a thing in time is "wara'" it. So the king and his seizing of the ship are "behind" the riding of those people in it, and Hell and its burning of the disbelievers comes after their disbelief and their deeds. This is like your saying: "Do such-and-such, and I am behind you as support," and like your saying as a threat: "I am behind you in pursuit," and similar. His, the Exalted, saying: "nor those they took" means by that the idols.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿This is guidance﴾ refers to the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir and ʿAsim, in the narration of Hafs, read "alimun" as an adjective of "ʿadhabun." This is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Mutarrif, and the people of Mecca. The rest read "alimin" as an adjective of "rijzin." This is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Isa, and al-A'mash. "Al-Rijz" is the most severe punishment. His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿and for them is a punishment﴾ is equivalent to your saying: "for them is a share." For this reason, and because of the difference between the two expressions, the saying ﴿a punishment of rijz﴾ is apt, since rijz is itself punishment.

So give him the tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And when he learns something of Our verses, he takes them in mockery. For those there is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿Before them lies Hell, and what they earned will not avail them at all, nor those they took as protectors besides Allah. For them is a tremendous punishment.﴾ ﴿This is guidance, and those who disbelieve in the verses of their Lord, for them is a punishment of painful wretchedness.﴾

"Al-Waylu" (woe) in the speech of the Arabs means calamities, sorrow, grief, distress, and hardship, among these meanings. It is a word used in invoking a curse upon a person. It has been narrated in some reports that in Hell there is a valley named Wayl. al-Tabari held that what is meant in the verse, and what the language requires, is an invocation against the people of falsehood and sin with the meanings mentioned earlier. Al-Affak is the great liar, the one from whom falsehood proceeds repeatedly. Al-Athim is an intensive form (ism fa'il of the intensive pattern) from athima, yref ya'thamu.

It has been narrated that the occasion of this verse was Abu Jahl; it was also said to be al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The correct view is that its occasion is what those mentioned and others did, and that it encompasses everyone who falls under the described attributes until the Day of Resurrection.

"Yusirru" means he remains firm upon his creed of disbelief. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿so give him the tidings of a painful punishment﴾ is apt, because it has made the punishment explicit; if the tidings were not restricted to anything, they would apply only to the beloved (ones).

If the matter is considered in terms of precedence or subsequence in existence, since time is like a path for things, the matter is consistent: whatever comes after a thing in time is "wara'" it. So the king and his seizing of the ship are "behind" the riding of those people in it, and Hell and its burning of the disbelievers comes after their disbelief and their deeds. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 45, verses 12–14:

The words of the Most High:

This is a verse of admonition concerning the sailing of the ship on the sea. Allah, exalted is He, subjected this great creation (p-593) to this small, weak creature. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"by His command"﴾, substitutes power and permission for the command to the sea and to the people in this matter. As for "seeking of the bounty of Allah", it is mostly by trade. Likewise, the aims of the land, such as pilgrimage and jihad, are also a seeking of bounty, and hunting in it is also a seeking of bounty.

As for "the subjection of what is in the heavens": it is the subjection of the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds, the winds, the air, and the angels entrusted with all of this. It is narrated that a certain righteous man had a guest who came to him, and he served him a loaf of bread. It seemed that the guest looked down upon it, so the host said to him: "Do not belittle it, for it did not become round until there were subjected to it, from the created beings and the angels, three hundred and sixty [things], among what we have mentioned of the creatures of the heavens, the angels, and the craftsmen of the children of Adam who bring about the rounding of the loaf." As for "the subjection of what is on the earth", it is the subjection of beasts, waters, valleys, mountains, and other things.

As for the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"all of it from Him"﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Every blessing is from Allah, Exalted is He." Most of the reciters read "minhu" (from Him), and it is a good pause. Maslama ibn Muharib read "mannuhu" with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the damma-vowelled nun, with the estimate: "huwa minhu" (it is from Him). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "minnatan" with a kasra on the mim, a fatha on the shadda-marked nun, and a fatha on the ta as a verbal noun. Abu Hatim said: the chain of this reading back to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is obscure. Abu al-Fath related it from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Jahdari, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Maslama ibn Muharib also read "minnatun" with a kasra on the mim and a damma on the ta.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse includes forgiveness in general, so it should be said that great matters such as killing and open disbelief and the like have had their forgiveness abrogated by the verse of the sword and the jizya and what the Sharia has definitively established. As for belittled matters such as harshness in speech and the like, it is possible that they be avoided as muhkam, and that pardoning them is closer to piety.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: When the verse ﴿"Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] was revealed, Finhas the Jew said: "The Lord of Muhammad has become needy, exalted is Allah above His saying!" So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, took his sword and went to kill him, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned him back and said: "Your Lord says: ﴿Say to those who believe: forgive﴾," and the verse.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an argument from it despite the earliness of its revelation. Makki and others mentioned that it was revealed in Mecca concerning 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he wanted to strike a polytheist who had insulted him. A more concise view in my opinion is that "qul" (say) is equivalent to: I urge the believers to forgiveness.

The explanation of this has been given more than once before.

The majority of reciters read "liyajziya" with the ya', meaning: that Allah may recompense. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and Ibn Wththab read "linajziya" with the nun. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' (in one narration from him) read "liyujza" in the passive form, ﴿"qawman"﴾ (a people), and this is on the basis that the estimate is: that the recompense may recompense a people. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 45, verses 15–17:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. Then to your Lord you will be returned.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, the judgment, and prophethood, and provided them with good things and preferred them over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We gave them clear proofs of the matter. And they did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual insolence. Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that in which they used to differ.﴾

Since it was established in the verse before this that Allah recompenses a people according to what they earn and punishes them for their sins and misdeeds, He affirmed that with His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul.﴾ His saying, "for his own soul" (fa-li-nafsihi), uses the lam of benefit (lam al-hazz), because the benefits and the things loved are expressed with the lam, which is the speech of the king. You say: "Affairs are facilitated for Zayd" (al-umur li-Zaydin mutaʼattiyah). The opposite is expressed with "ʻalā" (upon), so you say: "Affairs are difficult for so-and-so" (al-umur ʻala fulanin mustaʻsibah), and you say: "Zayd has wealth, and upon him is debt" (li-Zaydin mal wa-ʻalayhi dayn). Likewise, righteous deeds came here with the lam, and evil deeds with "ʻalā." His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ means: to His decree and His judgment.

The Scripture in His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave the Children of Israel the Scripture﴾ is the Torah, and "the judgment" (al-hukm) is the sunnah and jurisprudence (fiqh). It is said that the jurisprudence of rulings did not expand upon the tongue of any prophet as it expanded upon the tongue of Musa, peace be upon him. And "prophethood" (al-nubuwwah) refers to the fact that prophets among them were repeated, peace be upon them. His saying: ﴿and provided them with good things﴾ means: the lawful pleasurable things. With this the blessing is complete and its enumeration is fitting, and this is a reference to the manna and the quails, and the good things of al-Sham afterward, since it is the blessed land. The discussion of the meaning of "good things" has already been given, and a summary of the views of Malik and al-Shafiʻi on this has been stated. His saying (p-596): ﴿"over the worlds"﴾ intends: over the worlds of their time.

"The clear proofs of the matter" is the revelation through which the matters were detailed for them. Then Allah, exalted is He, pointed out their error and magnified it with His saying: ﴿And they did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual insolence﴾. That is because if they had differed through earnest striving in seeking the right, they would have had an excuse for the disagreement; but they differed out of insolence while the realities had become clear to them. Then He, exalted is He, threatened them by leaving their affair to His judgment between them on the Day of Resurrection.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implication of this speech is that the wording of the verse is a report. As for its wording, it indicates that it is the committing of disbelief, by the evidence of its being set in equivalence with belief. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 45, verses 22–24**

The Exalted said:

Who then will guide him after Allah? Will you not then take heed?﴾ ﴿And they say: "There is nothing but our life of this world. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time." But they have no knowledge of that; they only conjecture.﴾

It was said to one of the sages (al-Hukama'): "Why did Allah create the heavens and the earth?" He said: "To manifest the excellence of His workmanship." The *lam* (the particle "la-") in His words, glorified is He, "and so that (li-tujza)" appears to be the *lam* of purpose (lam kay), so that recompense is among the causes for the creation of the heavens and the earth. It may also be the *lam* of outcome (lam al-sayrura), meaning: the matter in them turned out such that some people were guided by them and others went astray from them, so that each person is recompensed according to his knowledge and what he has earned of good or evil.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿"Have you seen (a'ara'ayta)"﴾: some reciters softened the hamza, and a group pronounced it fully. Likewise it is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, lightened, and in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "a'ara'ayta" without a hamza. This verse is a consolation to Muhammad (ﷺ) concerning the disbelievers who turn away from faith; that is, do not hasten on their account and do not concern yourself with their affair, for there is no way for any human being to guide them, because Allah has led them astray. Ibn Jubayr said: ﴿"his god, his desire" (ilahahu hawahu)﴾ is a reference to idols, since they used to worship whatever stones they desired. Qatada said: the meaning is: he does not desire anything without pursuing it, not fearing Allah, the Exalted. This is like saying: "Desire is a worshipped god." Al-A'raj and Ibn Jubayr read "ilahatu hawahu" in the feminine, considering "ālihah" (gods). Although this verse was revealed concerning the desire for disbelief, it encompasses every desire of the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: Allah, the Exalted, mentions no "hawa" except in blame. Al-Sha'bi said: it was called "hawa" because of the bewilderment (hawiyya) of its owner. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The one who is incapable is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes for (things) from Allah." Sahl al-Tustari said: "Your desire is your disease; if you oppose it, it is your cure." Wahb said: "If you are in doubt between two matters, look at the one that is further from your desire, and go to it." And among the wisdom of poetry on this is the saying of one who said:

*When you do not disobey desire, desire will lead you*
*to everything in which there will be blame upon you.*

His words, the Exalted: ﴿"with knowledge (ala ilm)"﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is: with a knowledge from Allah that preceded. Another group said: that is, with knowledge of this misguidance, for the truth is what is left and turned away from. So the verse, on this interpretation (ta'wil), is among the verses of obstinacy, like His words, the Exalted: ﴿"And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them"﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. On both interpretations, His words "with knowledge" are a circumstantial clause (hal).

His words, the Exalted: ﴿"and He has set a seal upon his hearing and his heart, and placed a covering upon his sight"﴾ are all metaphors (isti'arat), for this misguided person does not benefit from what he hears, nor what he understands, nor what he sees, so he is, with these described attributes, as if he were... And this verse provides no proof for the Jabriyya (determinists), because the acquiring (taksib) is explicitly stated in it in His words, the Exalted: "took (ittakhadha)," and in His words, the Exalted: "with knowledge," on the last interpretation of it. Even if acquisition were not explicitly stated, it would still be intended in meaning. Most reciters read ﴿"covering (ghishawatan)"﴾ with a kasra on the ghayn. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read "ghashawatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, which is the dialect of Rabi'a. It is reported from al-Hasan and 'Ikrima "ghushawatan" with a damma on the ghayn, which is the dialect of 'Akl. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ghashwatan" with a fatha on the ghayn and sukun on the shin. His words, the Exalted: ﴿"from after Allah (min ba'di Allah)"﴾ contain an ellipsis of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), its estimated meaning being: "from after Allah's misguiding him." 'Asim, and I think al-Jahdari, read ﴿"tadhakkarun" (you take heed)﴾ with the dhal lightened. Most people read "tadhdhakkarun," also in the second person, with the dhal doubled. Al-A'mash read "tatadhakkarun" with two taas.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿"And they say: there is nothing but our life of this world" ...﴾ the verse is a quotation of the saying of some of the Quraysh. This is a naturalist (dahriyya) formulation of the disbelievers of the Arabs. The meaning of their words is: there is nothing in existence except this life in which we are, and there is no Hereafter and no resurrection.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of their words: ﴿"We die and we live"﴾. One group said: the meaning is: we are dead before we are brought into existence, then we live at the time of our existence. Another group said: the meaning is: we die when we are sperm and blood, then we live through the spirits in us; this is a view close to the first. On both views, mention of the well-known death, which is the departure of the soul from the body, drops out, and that is the most important thing to be mentioned. Another group said: the meaning is: we live and we die, so there is an inversion in the wording. Another group said: the purpose of the wording is to express the condition of the species (al-naw'), as if the species in its entirety were saying: "We are only that a group dies and a group lives, continually."

Their words: ﴿"And nothing destroys us but time (al-dahr)"﴾: that is, the length of the age, which is the destroyer, because the times are equal in its perfections. Allah, the Exalted, negated from them knowledge of this, and informed that these are conjectures from them and speculation that leads them to associate partners with Allah, the Exalted. "Al-dahr" and "al-zaman" are used by the Arabs with one meaning. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And nothing destroys us but a time that passes (dahrun yamurru)." Mujahid said: "al-dahr" here means time. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The people of the Jahiliyya used to say: 'Only the night and the day destroy us.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This usage differs from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not revile time, for Allah, the Exalted, is time." And in another hadith Allah, the Exalted, said: "The son of Adam reviles time, and I am time; in My hand are the night and the day." The meaning of this hadith is: Allah, the Exalted, is the One who does what you attribute to time and revile by its reviling. If examples of this in speech are considered, it will become apparent, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿"And they say: there is nothing but our life of this world" ...﴾ the verse is a quotation of the saying of some of the Quraysh. This is a naturalist (dahriyya) formulation of the disbelievers of the Arabs. The meaning of their words is: there is nothing in existence except this life in which we are, and there is no Hereafter and no resurrection.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of their words: ﴿"We die and we live"﴾. One group said: the meaning is: we are dead before we are brought into existence, then we live at the time of our existence. Another group said: the meaning is: we die when we are sperm and blood, then we live through the spirits in us; this is a view close to the first. Another group said: the meaning is: we live and we die, so there is an inversion in the wording. Another group said: the purpose of the wording is to express the condition of the species (al-naw'), as if the species in its entirety were saying: "We are only that a group dies and a group lives, continually."

Their words: ﴿"And nothing destroys us but time (al-dahr)"﴾: that is, the length of the age, which is the destroyer, because the times are equal in its perfections. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This usage differs from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not revile time, for Allah, the Exalted, is time." The meaning of this hadith is: Allah, the Exalted, is the One who does what you attribute to time and revile by its reviling. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 45, verse 30–33:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord will admit them into His mercy. That is the manifest triumph.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved: "Were My verses not recited to you? But you were arrogant, and you were a criminal people."﴾ ﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt in it," you said, "We do not know what the Hour is. We only assume an assumption, and we are not certain."﴾ ﴿And the evils of what they did will appear to them, and what they used to mock will encompass them.﴾

Allah, blessed and exalted, mentioned the condition of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, and joined them in the mention so that the matter becomes clear in the mind of the listener, for things are made clear by mentioning their opposites alongside them. Al-fawz (triumph) is the attainment of the desired goal.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿As for those who disbelieved, were not...﴾ [there is an omission in it]: the implied sense is: "As for those who disbelieved, it will be said to them: Were not...?" So "it will be said to them" (yuqalu lahum) was omitted for brevity, and the fa' remained indicating the response that "amma" requires. Then the interrogative alif was placed before it, since the interrogative has precedence in speech in every case. Allah made the disbelievers stand accountable for arrogance, because it is among the worst of traits.

Hamzah alone read "wal-sa'ata" (and the Hour) in the accusative, as a conjunction with His saying ﴿the promise of Allah﴾. It was also narrated from Abu 'Amr, 'Isa, and al-A'mash. Ibn Mas'ud read "ḥaqqun wa-inna al-sa'ata la rayba fīhā," and al-A'mash also read it this way. The rest read "wal-sa'atu" in the nominative, and there are two possible grounds for this: the first is that it is a new inceptive statement (al-ibtida' wal-istinaf); the second is that it is a conjunction upon the position of "inna" and what it governs, because the implied sense is "the promise of Allah is true." This was stated by Abu 'Ali in al-Hujja. Some grammarians said: one does not conjoin upon the position of "inna" except when the operator that inna nullified remains in effect. Likewise is the position of the bā' in his saying:

"... so we are not with the mountains nor with the iron"

Since "laysa" is negating, conjoining upon the position before the entry of the bā' is permissible. Something of this view appears in the Kitab of Sibawayh, but we have mentioned what Abu 'Ali related, and he is the model to follow.

As for their saying ﴿we only assume an assumption﴾, its meaning is: we only assume after the acceptance of your report, and it does not give us certainty.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the evils appeared to them﴾ and the verse...: it is a depiction of the condition of the Day of Resurrection. "Ḥāqa" means: descended and encompassed, and it is used for what is disliked. In His saying ﴿"mā kānū"﴾ there is an omitted genitive (muḍāf): its estimated form is "the recompense of what they used to do," i.e., the punishment for their being those who mocked.

So today they will not be brought out of it, nor will they be allowed to make amends.﴾ ﴿So to Allah belongs all praise, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs greatness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Its meaning, *nansākum* (نَنْساكم, "We forget you"): We will leave you (نَتْرُكُكم) as you left (تَرَكْتُمْ) the meeting of this your Day. You made no preparation for it (فَلَمْ يَقَعْ مِنكُمُ اسْتِعْدادٌ لَهُ) and did not get ready (ولا تَأهَّبْتُمْ). Thus the punishment in this verse is named by the name of the sin.

*Al-ma'wā* (المَأْوى, "the dwelling") is the place where a person lives and spends most or all of his time.

*Āyāt Allāh* (آياتِ اللهِ, "the signs of Allah") is a comprehensive term that includes the verses of the Qur'an and the proofs (الأدِلَّةِ) that Allah established for His servants to reflect upon.

Most of the readers of the recitations (qirā'āt, القراءات, the varying canonical modes of reciting the Qur'an) read *lā yakhrujūna* (لا يَخْرُجُونَ) with a *ḍamma* on the yā' (which is dotted from below) and a *fatḥa* on the rā', meaning "they are not brought out." Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Ibn Wathhāb, al-A'mash and al-Ḥasan read *lā yakhrujūna* with the verb ascribed to them, with a *fatḥa* on the yā' and a *ḍamma* on the rā', meaning "they do not go out."

*Yusta'tabūna* (يُسْتَعْتَبُونَ, "they are allowed to make amends") means they are asked to return (تَطَلَّبَ مِنهم مُراجَعَةً) to righteous action.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So to Allah belongs all praise﴾ through to the end of the surah, is praise of Him, Exalted is He, and affirmation of His divinity. In this there is a refutation of the matter of idols and idolatrous stones (al-aṣnām wa'l-anṣāb). The common reading is *rabbi* (رَبِّ, "Lord") with a *kasra* in all three places, as an adjective (عَلى الصِفَةِ). Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a *ḍamma* in them, meaning "He is Lord" (هو رَبٌّ).
